text: Xiao Yan knelt before the stone tablet. In the older books his name was spelled Hsiao Yen, but he had stopped caring about spellings long ago. “Xiao Yan-ge,” called a girl from the courtyard, and Ling ran up with a basket of pills. “Ling, you should be resting,” he said. “The Alchemist Guild will want its debt paid by autumn,” she answered. Sect rules were strict that year. The sect master of Jade Cloud Peak had forbidden every outside pill.

Two clans shared the river valley, and each had a clan head. The clan head of the Lu clan was a patient man. The clan head of the Shen clan was not. When Lu Chen arrived, Shen Hu slammed the table. “Your clan head insults us!” “Mine?” said Lu Chen. “Ask yours about the stolen grain.” Neither of them noticed Sung slipping out through the back door with the ledger. Silence followed, and then a distant bell from Nine Dragon Temple marked the hour.

Heaven punishes the arrogant, the saying goes, but Wei Ming had never seen it happen. He climbed the last step and found Ancestor Hong sitting beneath a pine, eating a plain steamed bun. “Sit,” said Ancestor Hong. “You carry the Black Tortoise Seal. Did Mister Du give it to you?” “He did.” The old man laughed. “Then Wei Ming, you are late. The Dao Society meets at dusk, and Chapter Nine of its rules is very clear.”

Grace was a word the village used for harvest, but here it was the name of a girl. Grace Tan carried water up the ridge to Wolf Fang Camp. Behind her walked Tan Jie, her elder sister, whom the soldiers called Second Miss Tan. “Tan-jie,” Grace said, “is it true the Iron Banner Army will march at dawn?” “Ask the general.” At night the two sisters shared a cold meal. The commander, known only as the General, never learned that either of them could read maps.

Sima Lan wrote his own name three ways on the wall: Sima Lan, Ssu-ma Lan, and Lan Sima, as the foreigners said it. Then he rubbed all three out. “Master Sima,” a servant whispered, “the envoy from Vermilion Bird Court waits.” “Let the envoy wait.” In the corridor stood Wang Er, bound by hemp rope. “Wang Er was captured at Broken Bridge,” said the guard. “Good,” said Sima Lan. “Then the Jade Emperor's Decree is safe.” Perhaps.

Will was the one thing the mountain could not take from Will Chen. He climbed anyway. His teacher, Teacher Gu, called him Chen Wei when angry and Little Will when pleased, and both names meant the same boy. At the summit stood the Ice Soul Pagoda. Inside waited the Pagoda Keeper, who asked only one question: “What do you want?” “To return the Moon Pearl,” said Chen Wei. The keeper smiled. Past that smile, the wind of Mount Xuan howled.

Beauty was a trap, and Mei knew it. At the Hundred Flowers Sect she was called Junior Sister Mei; in the capital, Lady Mei; in the old stories, the Plum Blossom Swordswoman. All three were one woman. “Mei-jie!” cried a young disciple, “the sect master wants you at Plum Hall.” She tied her hair and took up the sword Winter Whisper. Nobody on the road recognised her, which was exactly how she wanted it.

The two brothers walked beneath Heaven's Gate, a pass in the cliffs. Gu Yan was the elder, and the villagers said Gu Yan-ge with respect. Gu Bo was the younger. “Eldest,” Gu Bo teased, “when will the Longevity Sect let us in?” “When the Patriarch dies,” said Gu Yan. “Hush. Heaven hears.” Neither brother carried more than a rice bag and a cracked flute, the Bone Flute, which had once belonged to their mother. Stars rose over Qilian Pass.

Nothing in the sutra mentioned Cang Ming. Still, the monks of Silent Bell Temple spoke of him in whispers: Cang Ming, Tsang Ming, the Blind Monk. Three days earlier, Abbot Kong had died; now the abbot's seat stood empty. “Who will lead?” asked Novice Pei. Nobody answered. The wind carried incense across the courtyard of Lingyin, and the great bell, Thunder Mother, rang once by itself. Chapter Seven of the monastery rules says: a bell that rings unprompted is an omen.

The guild hall of Seongsu smelled of rust. Yoo Joonghyuk stood by the window, and the clerk, who liked old spellings, wrote Yu Jung-hyeok in the ledger. “Joonghyuk-ssi, the Hunters Association wants a word.” He did not turn. Another hunter called him the Regressor, and the trainees whispered Captain Yoo. All three were one tired man. Rain hammered the glass. “Tell them I am busy,” he said, and picked up the dagger known as Black Fang.

Two headmasters shared the island school. The headmaster of Haneul Academy was strict. The headmaster of Bada Academy was kind, and everyone preferred him. When Park Min-ho arrived with his transfer papers, Min-ho was handed to the strict one. “Park Minho?” the secretary asked, spelling it the other way. “Yes.” A bell rang over the harbour. In the hallway, Ji-woo stood waiting with a mop, pretending she had not heard a thing.

Nobody called her by her name. Rumours named her Lee Seo-yeon, the guild's accountant, but the hunters said Seoyeon-nim, and the children said Aunt Lee. Winter came early to Gangnam. “Seo-yeon unnie is late,” sighed Hana, and set out the cups. On the shelf lay the contract for the Blue Dragon Dungeon, stamped with the seal of the Cheongryong Company. The old chairman had signed it with a shaking hand.

Will it hold? Will Han asked himself at the barrier. He was only half Korean, and everyone used his English name. His mother, Han Eun-ji, called him Wooyoung at home. “Wooyoung-ah, eat.” At the academy his rival, Seo Hyun, called him Han Will to annoy him. The Black Turtle Society had sent a letter that morning. Nobody opened it. Snow settled on Mount Bukhan.

“Brother,” said Taeyang, “the Tower opens tonight.” Tae-yang was nineteen and spoke too quickly. His elder, Cha Hyun-woo, was known on the forums as Hyun and in the guild as the Wall. “The Tower is not a game.” “Hyun-nim,” said the receptionist, “the Floor Ten gate is yours.” The old master of the Iron Lotus Guild was watching from the balcony, saying nothing.

Choi Ha-rin was eleven when the Gate opened over Incheon. Years later the papers wrote Ha-rin Choi, the foreigners wrote Harin Choi, and the soldiers called her the Little General. “Harin-ssi, the Ministry on the phone.” “Tell them I am training.” The sword on her back was Daybreak, a gift from her father. Hunters bowed as she passed the Hunters' Hall. She hated it.

The regressor's notebook listed names in two spellings: Yoon Se-ah / Yun Sea, Baek Do-hyun / Paik Dohyun. He never knew which the system preferred. “Seah-ssi,” he began. “Call me Captain,” she said. “Everyone else does.” The two stood at the edge of Hangang Park. Behind them, the Moonlight Guild was burying its dead. “And Dohyun?” “Missing.” Nothing more was said, but the notebook stayed open.

Hunter was what the old woman called her grandson, after the sign on his jacket. Hunter was no nickname; it was on his registration card. At the clinic of Saebyeok Hospital a nurse asked, “Hunter Jung?” and the grandson sighed. His real name, Jung Han-gyeol, appeared only in the grandmother's prayers. The Pale Sun Church sent flowers. “Hangyeol-ssi,” the doctor said, “the scan is clear.”

In the north valley, Elder Moon kept bees. In the south valley, another Elder Moon kept goats. They had shared a name since birth but never a conversation. When the Council of Nine Peaks summoned the elders, both came, and sat three seats apart. “Moon Il-sun,” said the speaker, and one stood. “Not you,” he added, and the other, Moon Il-seong, rose in a huff. The honey cake on the table was called Sleeping Dragon.

Haruto woke in an unfamiliar bed. A girl with silver hair bowed. “Haruto-sama, the Demon King awaits.” “Who?” “His Majesty.” Everyone in the castle of Shirogane used these three expressions for one man, whose true name, Zenobel Karst, was never spoken. Haruto Kisaragi sat up slowly. The sword by his bed was Dawn Cleaver. He had no idea how it got there, nor why the Adventurers' Guild was waiting downstairs.

Hope? There was none, said Hope, the stray cat, to nobody. Nozomi, which means the same thing, scratched her ear. “Nozomi-san, breakfast.” “I'm coming.” Beyond the garden wall lay Sakura Ward, full of people who believed in luck. Nozomi did not. She worked at the Lantern Bookshop and wrote letters for the elderly. A man in a grey coat, called Sensei by the neighbours, visited every Friday and paid in oranges.

Mizuki ran. Behind her, the Shadow Court howled. Sentence by sentence her breath grew shorter; the corridors of Ryuuzen Castle twisted. She remembered her mother's advice: do not look back. At the great hall waited the shrine maiden, the one whom the villagers revered as Miko-sama and whom the court clerks recorded as Lady Hinako. Hinako smiled. “Mizuki-chan, you came.” In her hands lay the Mirror of Nine Clouds, cold and bright.

Ichigo was also a fruit, and everyone made the joke. Ichigo Aoyama ignored them. At the dojo of Bright Pine, the master, Master Sato, called him Aoyama-kun while the older boys called him Strawberry. All three names meant the same sullen boy, who held a bamboo sword like a weapon. “Again,” said Sato-sensei. Dust rose from the floor. Outside the gate of Nagano, snow began to fall.

Nothing was left of Black Rose Manor but chimneys. Lord Ashikaga walked through the ash, with his retainer Kenji a step behind. “Ashikaga-sama, the Imperial Court sent no word.” “It will.” The two never spoke of the fire. “Kenji, bring the Iron Fan.” “Yes, my lord.” Whoever had set the fire had left a single paper crane on the doorstep, folded in the style of the Hidden Leaf Order.

Aiko, Akio, and Akira ran the shop together. Customers constantly mixed up the three. “Aiko-san, two buns!” “I'm Akio,” grumbled the man at the counter. The shop was called Three Pines, and it sat in the lane behind Tsukimi Station. Their landlord, the old man who owned half the street and was known to the neighbours as Landlord Mori, collected rent every month. “Tell Akira he owes me tea,” he muttered.

“Tsubasa, wake up.” Tsubasa Arai groaned. The morning sun lit the room of the dormitory at Fujimori Academy. Heaven, he thought, was a long weekend. “Arai-kun, assembly!” His roommate, Sota, tossed him a tie. In the hallway, the vice-principal was already collecting late students. “Sota-kun,” she said, “you too.” Neither noticed the strange letter sealed with the mark of the Crimson Moon.

In village Hanabi, two elders kept the shrine. Elder Tsuda, the tall one, and another Elder Tsuda, the small one, were unrelated and bore the same surname by accident of history. “Tsuda-sama,” said the pilgrim, bowing, “which of you holds the Heron Scroll?” “Neither,” said both. The shrine guardian, a fox spirit known as Inari-sama, yawned in her sleep. Wind rattled the Gate of Ten Thousand Lanterns.

The student known as Yamato never gave his surname, so some wrote Yamato Kuze and others Kuze Yamato. Both were him. In Kyoto, where he lived, they said Kuze-san; online, he was Night Hawk. “Yamato, the Seventh Division called,” said Captain Reiji. “They want you.” “For what?” “For the sword.” He touched Kusanagi's Shadow and thought of home. Rain began to fall on the roofs of the old city.

Arjun waited under the banyan tree outside Hastinapur Fort. “Arjun-ji,” said the gatekeeper, “the maharaj will see you now.” The old king had two sons, and each was called Yuvraj by his own faction. “Which one?” asked Arjun. The guard shrugged. Hope was a luxury in that court. Far off, a conch sounded from the Sun Temple. Guruji had warned him: speak little, bow low, and keep the bow named Moon Arrow hidden beneath your cloak.

Priya Sharma dropped her bag in the hall. “Sharma-ji's daughter is back,” the neighbours whispered, and “Priya-didi!” cried the children. To her father she was only Beti. In Lajpat Nagar, everyone knew the family on the corner, and there were three households of that surname on the same street, none related. “Which Sharma-ji?” someone always asked. The tea at the corner stall, Chai Wala Raju's famous brew, steamed beside the door of the Lotus Cooperative Bank.

Joy was the nickname of Joydeep Ghosh, and in the lanes of Kolkata he was Joy-da to every child. “Joy-da, the cinema!” “Not today.” His friend Mitra called him Joydeep-babu to tease him. Rain had turned the road to mud. At the Bengal Film Society they showed old reels, and the projectionist, Mr. Dutta, knew every frame. “Dutta-babu,” whispered Joy, “do you have the lost reel?” The old man smiled and tapped a tin marked Midnight Raga.

“Hunter,” said Rani Devi, “is what the British called him.” Hunter was in fact a Gurkha scout named Bahadur Thapa. The queen of Jhansi used a third name for him, Chhoti Tope. In the court of Rani Devi each name meant one man. Dust blew along the walls of the Red Fort of Jhansi. “Bahadur-ji,” said the queen, “have the cannons ready.” He bowed. The silver sword named Lakshmi's Edge hung at her hip.

Vikram sat in the audience of the Mumbai Sabha with his hand raised. “Vikram-ji, your question?” “Respected Chairperson, my question is about water.” The chairperson was Smt. Kapoor, known in the press as the Iron Lady of Dadar. Laughter rippled. The hall at Shivaji Park was packed. “Vikram bhai,” someone said, “sit down.” “Water first,” said Vikram. It was the oldest argument in the city.

Lakshmi walked into the kitchen and found her grandmother already awake. “Ammamma,” she said, “the Bank of Madras sent a letter.” The old woman did not look up. “Read it, Lakshmi-kutty.” The letter said that the family house in Mylapore, called Anandam, would be sold at auction. Ammamma folded her hands. Sentimental objects, like the brass vessel Kamadhenu, cannot be put on a ledger. “Then we will see,” she said.

Two priests in Varanasi answered to Panditji. The first, Pandit Shastri, taught at the ghat. The second, Pandit Joshi, kept the temple of Kashi Vishwanath. A pilgrim asked, “Panditji, where may I pray?” “Which?” they both said. The pilgrim, Rohan, bowed in confusion. Smoke rose from the ghat, and a boatman called Kallu laughed at them all. Near the boat lay a conch known as the Voice of Ganga, silent.

Sunita and Sunil opened the shop on Linking Road. People said Sunita-ji was the shrewder. “Ji,” said a customer, “which saree is best?” “Ask Sunil.” The business was called Sun & Moon Silks, though neither of them wanted the moon. The landlord, a quiet Parsi called Mr. Dastur, collected the rent. On the shelf, between rolls of cloth, lay a carved box named Peacock's Secret. Nobody had ever opened it.

“Kabir!” called Maa from the courtyard. “Eat!” The family compound in Lucknow held three generations, and each had a different name for the same boy: Kabir to his mother, Kabir Khan on paper, Chhotu to the cousins. At the Imambara Trust, an old clerk stamped his admission form. “Khan-sahab,” the clerk said, “welcome.” Outside, pigeons rose from the roof of the Bara Imambara. Kabir ran toward the gate, carrying a worn toy named Pagal Ghoda.

Mr. Ashworth was not pleased to find a stranger in the library at Thornfield Hall. “Ashworth,” said the visitor, “I am Captain Hale, and your sister has invited me.” The housekeeper, Mrs. Penrose, curtsied. Hope of a quiet evening faded. In the village the squire was thought stern, and the vicar kind. Between them they ruled Little Wickham, and the Wickham Charity Society met every Thursday. Hale set down his hat.

Grace brought the tea. Grace Alder had served at Hartley Abbey for eleven years and knew every cough in the house. “Miss Alder,” said the new maid, “the mistress is asking.” “Which one?” There were two mistresses: Lady Hartley, and her sister-in-law, who was also Lady Hartley. “The younger.” Grace straightened her apron. The Hartley Trust had changed hands that spring, and no servant yet knew the new terms.

Dmitri Volkov crossed the square in Novgorod with his collar up. His friends said Dima; his enemies said Volkov; the old babushka at the stall said Dmitri Ivanovich. The tsar's agent was watching from the bell tower. “Comrade Volkov,” called a soldier, “the commissar will see you.” The Red Lantern Society kept its papers in a cellar below the cathedral, and the key was an iron fish called Silver Pike. Snow squeaked beneath his boots.

Sun was a rare name in Reykjavik, and Sun Gunnarsdottir was used to the questions. “Sun Gunnarsdottir?” the customs officer repeated. “Yes.” Her grandmother, Amma Gudrun, had picked it. In the harbour, the ship Northern Ember rocked. The head of the Fishermen's Union, a gruff man known as the Captain, waved from the dock. “Gunnarsdottir! Get aboard.” Sea wind snapped the flags of Faxafloi.

Two lighthouse keepers shared the rock of Skerry Head. The elder was Old Tam; the younger was also called Tam, and the harbourmaster, Mr. Gillespie, gave up and named them by their lamps. Hunter was the terrier, and he belonged to neither. “Hunter!” cried both keepers at once. The Northern Lights Board sent its inspector every spring. Heaven knows what he made of the place. He wrote in his report: “Two Tams, one dog, one lamp.”

Elara Voss opened the letter at breakfast. Dr. Voss was a physician in Vienna, and her father, Herr Voss, practised in Graz. Both were referred to as Doktor Voss, and the postman sorted their post by guess. “Fraulein Voss,” said the maid, “it is the university.” The letter named her to the chair of the Imperial Academy of Medicine. Elara read it twice, then folded it into the pocket of her coat beside the silver watch Mnemosyne.

Joy was the family dog of the Okafor-Lindqvist household, and also the mother's name. Joy Lindqvist laughed when the vet called, “Joy? Which?” At the clinic of St. Olaf's Vet, Dr. Berglund was patient. “Both, then. Joy the dog first.” Outside, the city council was voting on a leash law. The mayor, Nils Berg, was known as the Leash Man. Fog crept over Gothenburg, and the harbour bells sounded like cracked teacups.

Katarzyna Nowak, called Kasia by friends and Pani Nowak by students, taught at Jagiellonian Lyceum in Krakow. Kasia kept a wooden crow named Wawel on her desk. “Pani Kasia,” said a boy, “is it true the rector is leaving?” “Ask Mr. Wisniewski.” “He says ask you.” She sighed. The two men had been feuding for years, and everyone in Krakow knew it. Chapter by chapter, she wrote their quarrel in her private diary.

Edmund and Edmond Fairweather were twins, and Mr. Fairweather was therefore either. “Fairweather!” called the coachman. Both turned. “The one with the hat.” Edmund sighed and took off his hat. The twins ran the firm of Fairweather & Fairweather in Bristol, where the clerks wrote E. Fairweather on every memo and prayed. The firm's seal, The Twin Gulls, was a source of constant quarrel, being a single ring.

Vael'thar drew his blade beneath the twin moons of Ixomir. The Ashen Concord had marched for nine days, and the Concordat, as the soldiers called their commander, was weary. “Vael'thar,” said Oryn Dask, “the Glass Throne is not worth the ruin.” “Nothing is.” Behind them a horn sounded from the walls of Ixomir. The old captain, called Dask by his friends and Captain Oryn by his men, readied the standard.

The spire of Quel-Anor was empty. Nyssa Thorne climbed it anyway, and the Warden of the spire watched from a window. “Thorne,” he said, “you carry the Silver Lathe?” “I do.” “Then you are the one the Order of Quiet Hands foretold.” She shrugged. Sentences like that always meant trouble. Hope, she thought, was a fine sentiment for people with fewer enemies. Below, Brother Calum sang an old dirge to the stones.

Two tribes shared the salt flats of Orrovan, and each had a chieftain. The chieftain of the Sand Hawks was named Brak Uum. The chieftain of the Red Herons was named Sethra Quill. Neither would sit first. “Brak,” murmured an elder, “the water-bearers wait.” “Let Quill begin.” “Let the Hawk begin,” she answered, meaning him. Wind blew grit across the tents. The sacred bowl, Mother of Rain, waited between them, empty.

“Hunter, wake.” Hunter Rhoss opened his eyes in the cold of the ship Argent Wake. He had been a bounty man on Kellan Prime, and the crew still called him Hunter, though the Provost used his surname. “Rhoss,” said the Provost, “the Helix Authority has issued a warrant.” “Naturally.” He reached for the pistol named Quiet Debt. Outside, the stars wheeled past the hull like cold coins.

Maelis and Maelor were twins born under the same eclipse. The Seer of Embers had warned the court: one would be Queen, the other Queen, and the realm would split. “Maelis,” whispered the nurse, “you are the elder.” “And Maelor?” “The cleverer.” In the great hall of Karthuun, the Court of Veils gathered in grey silks. The two girls clasped hands. Between them hung the crown called Dawnthorn.

Rain was an unusual name for a dwarf, but Rain Hammerfell bore it proudly. “Hammerfell!” called the foreman, Boss Tuck. “The forge at Deepdelve is cold!” “Then light it, Tuck.” The Stonebeard Clan sent a messenger. “Rain-of-the-Hammer,” he said, using the old style, “your clan head requests you.” She wiped her hands. The anvil, Old Mother, rang with a note like laughter, and the cavern answered.

Tessaly kept the lighthouse of Mirren Point, and the sailors called her the Lamp Keeper. Her real name, Tessaly Vane, appeared only on the charts. “Vane!” cried the captain of the Sable Heron, a ship battered by storm. “Light the beacon!” “It is lit,” she said. A moment later the wind snapped the shutters, and Tessaly smiled. Somewhere above, the Tidewatch League had struck its colours and gone home, forgetting her.

Pip and Joy were the two smallest scouts of the Lantern Company, and the only ones the captain trusted with keys. “Pip,” said Joy, “are we lost?” “Never.” They stood in the ruined plaza of Orsellin, where a statue of Lord Haskell had lost its head. Sergeant Mose called from the rear: “Scouts! The Moth Gate is open!” Neither scout moved. The key, Pale Truth, hung warm against Pip's chest.

Zhorel, Zhorell, and Jorel were the same man: a smuggler on Thessen Dock, whose name changed with each port's accent. “Captain Zhorel,” said the pilot. “Mister Jorel,” said the customs man. “Old Z,” said his crew. The Salt Syndicate wanted a word. He ignored it. In his coat pocket lay a small iron whistle, Thrush Call, that could summon any ship in the harbour. He stroked it, and smiled at the wet horizon.

Elena Petrova met Wang Lei outside the conference hall in Singapore. “Dr. Petrova,” he said, “Prof. Okonkwo sends regards.” “Wang-laoshi, please.” “Lei is fine.” The Pacific Biotech Forum had invited three hundred guests, and two of them carried the same family name, Okonkwo. Nobody could tell which Okonkwo was speaking at ten. “Hope you slept,” laughed Elena. Rain pounded the glass.

Heaven and earth were quiet. Luo Qing, a cultivator from Cloud Peak, had somehow been summoned to the kingdom of Elmoria, where Sir Percival called him Lord Luo. “Which Luo?” asked the king. “Luo Qing,” said the knight. “Qing-ge,” whispered a servant. The Royal Order of the Rose had never met a sect elder. The sword he carried, Frost Whisper, hummed with confusion. The king, called His Majesty by court and Old Hal by his wife, laughed.

Joy and Hope worked at the same ward of St. Anne's Hospital. Joy Mukherjee and Hope Park were friends. “Nurse Joy,” called a patient, “Nurse Hope says come.” The doctor, Dr. Tanaka, laughed. “Mukherjee-san, Park-ssi, the ward round.” The head nurse, a stern woman known as Matron Okoye, inspected beds. On the wall hung a poster for the Global Health Alliance. Rain streaked the windows, and a baby cried.

Sun and Moon were the names of two market cats in Marrakesh, and also of two clerks at the Souk Trading Company. Sun and Moon shared a desk. “Sun,” said Mr. Haddad, “where is Moon?” “Feeding the cats.” “Which?” “Both.” The director of the company, a thin man called Si Bensouda, smiled at the confusion. Through the arch of Bab Agnaou came the smell of cumin and rain.

Sophie Laurent translated the old chronicle. In it, a sect master named Wu Han befriended a Sultan, Harun, and a Viking, Eirik. Odd company, she thought, and sure to be invented. At the Sorbonne Library, her colleague Prof. Dubois disagreed. “Dubois,” she said, “look at the Silk Road Ledger. Three scripts, one hand.” “Sophie-san,” he joked, “you are too clever.” Outside, snow dusted the roofs of Paris, and the clock tower struck noon.

Master Yin and Sister Maria shared the courtyard of the Lotus and Cross Mission. The monastery's old bell, Gentle Thunder, marked hours for both. “Yin-shifu,” said the novice, Brother Tomas, “the rain has soaked the garden.” “Maria will mend it.” “Sister is mending the roof.” The abbot of the Cross wing and the abbot of the Lotus wing met at supper and said nothing. Over Hanoi, the evening clouds were purple.
